question: Is it permissible for a female teacher to teach boys at a coeducational school?
asked: A sister comes from a land where schooling is gender segregated and women typically do not teach at co-educational schools. She has moved to a land where co-education is the norm. She is a school teacher, only accustomed to teaching girls, and now feels shy. Is there any Islamic prohibition on her teaching young men?
answer:
The issue of intermixing of the genders, the intermixing of men and women, is one where the Shari'ah has some guidelines, and then the Shari'ah allows the rest of it to be dictated by culture. This is a very important point. In some aspects the Shari'ah takes complete control, and it will tell you: do this and don't do that. In other aspects the Shari'ah will be silent and culture will dictate. And in some, there's a little bit of Shari'ah mixed in, and the rest of it will be culture. And intermixing of the genders is one such area where the Shari'ah has some guidelines and then the rest can be culture-sensitive. In other words, if you fulfill the Shar'i guidelines, the rest is going to be dependent on the culture of the land that you live in.

And so we have, for example, from the Shari'ah, when it comes to intermixing, when it comes to men and women interacting together, some very simple guidelines. And of the most important guidelines, as the Prophet ﷺ said: let no man enter upon a lady whose husband is absent, meaning he's gone on a journey. Because remember, in those days the man would go for many weeks or months on end, and so the lady would be left alone in the house. So the Prophet ﷺ said: let no man enter into the house of somebody who has gone traveling, and his wife is there, absent from her husband, except that he has another man with him. So nobody should enter the house of a lady. For example, somebody has to deliver some food, somebody has to deliver groceries, somebody has to service something of the house. So nobody should enter in alone. There should not be privacy. There should be somebody there that is also with the person, so that everybody maintains a decorum and a proper characteristic.

Also, we know that the Shari'ah has forbidden khalwa, and khalwa means that a man and a woman that are obviously not related to one another are alone in a place that nobody has access to: a closed room or something of this nature. This is considered khalwa. The Shari'ah also has guidelines with regards to dress, with regards to interactions. Both genders have to be dressed appropriately. Both genders have to act in a dignified manner, avoid flirtatious talk, speak in a manner that gives the sense of gravitas and decorum that is appropriate for our religion of Islam. Because we all understand the reasons why these laws have come: we protect the institution of marriage; we do not open up any doors of evil.

Now, given all of these laws, beyond this, how much can the two genders interact and mix together? For example, can families come together, couples, friends come together, and they're sitting together at the same dining table, various friends and their husbands and wives all come together and they're sitting at the same dining table? Believe it or not, this is culture-sensitive. And I know some of my viewers have never heard of this: why is this question even being asked? And again, the more you travel, the more you live in different cultures, the more you understand that different societies have different norms.

For example, in more conservative lands like Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, it is very, very rare, almost unheard of, for genders to be interacting together. And that in and of itself is neither Islamic nor un-Islamic. That is the way that that culture is. Frankly, if you read the seerah, if you read the books of early Islam, the Sahabah had a level of interaction that was definitely more than the level of interaction that takes place in many of the Gulf countries in our times. In public, in the marketplace, in the bazaars, in the masajid, men and women knew each other by their first names, and they would address one another in public and ask a question that needed to be asked. There was no shame or harm in doing that. In our times, in those societies, it is completely taboo. It is unheard of that a person is going to address somebody outside of his or her immediate family.

And again, I'm not saying that's right, I'm not saying that's wrong. I'm simply telling you the status quo; that is the way that it is in those lands. And what I am saying is that the Shari'ah allows cultures to take charge, and to go sometimes on the more segregational side between genders, and sometimes on the less segregational, as long as its barriers are met.

And in fact, this difference goes back to the very beginning of Islam, and it goes back to the cultures and societies in the early days of Islam. In the famous book, the Muwatta of Imam Malik, which is the earliest book of hadith that has been written, or one of the earliest books of hadith (Imam Malik died 179 Hijrah), a man asked Imam Malik, basically, can a man and his wife sit with a guest and entertain them at the same dinner table? So somebody has come, and the wife and husband are sitting there: can they eat together, partake of the meal together? And Imam Malik said there is no sin, there is no haraj, there is no problem in this, as long as it is the custom of their people to do so. And in Medina at that time it was the custom to do so. It wasn't an issue that men and women, as long as they're dressed appropriately, are sitting at the same... well, obviously they didn't have a table, tables came later on, but they're sitting in the same area, and they're sitting together to eat.

Now, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal heard or read this anecdote from Imam Malik. Imam Ahmad was in Baghdad. This is a hundred years, a little bit more than a hundred years later... not quite 100, but around 80 years after this. So Imam Ahmad heard of this anecdote many decades later, and he read of this, and he was in Baghdad. And in Baghdad, because of the culture and because of the wealth... And by the way, another issue: it's not the rule of thumb, but generally speaking, the more wealth and the more privilege that came in those societies, the more segregation was possible, and the more rudimentary type of lifestyle didn't allow for that type of segregation.

So Baghdad is now the capital of the world, not just the Muslim world. It is the political and intellectual and economic capital of the world. It is the largest city, the wealthiest city, by the time of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. And so Imam Ahmad heard or read of this, and, the narration goes, ta'ajjab: he was amazed, he was astonished. Like, "Wow, Imam Malik allowed this?" Because in his time, in his place, it was unheard of that men and women who were not related to one another would sit at the same place and then partake of that meal. So Imam Ahmad understood that's a different culture, and in our culture in Baghdad, that is something that is not going to happen.

So this is something that does vary from time to place to culture to civilization. And therefore, as long as the Islamic rulings are met, which is appropriate interactions, appropriate dressing, everything that the Shari'ah has asked, no khalwa, all of this is done, the rest, as we said, is culture-sensitive.

So this sister asks, our sister Najwa... I'm assuming she's coming from a Gulf country, because that's really generally where education is completely segregated, and now she is living in a land where it is not segregated. So she's asking, is there a Shar'i prohibition? And the response is that **there is no Shar'i prohibition per se**, as long as she is dressed appropriately, and the interactions, inshallah, I'm assuming obviously, will all be done in a manner that is dictated by the Shari'ah. In and of itself, there is no haraj or problem with men and women interacting in public in a dignified manner.

And by the way, Imam al-Nawawi mentions this in his book al-Majmu'. Imam al-Nawawi mentions that al-ikhtilat of men and women, the mixing of men and women, is not haram in and of itself, as long as it is not done in khalwa, as long as it is not one man and one woman mixing in privacy, or being alone in the privacy of a house or something. Then this is not something that is haram per se. This is Imam al-Nawawi writing. There's nothing wrong with men and women being in public together, interacting together in public. That's not haram per se.

That having been said, in me having said this, I also have to add the caveat, which is that plenty of studies have shown that, especially in the adolescence phase, it is in fact better for young men and young women to be separated during the educational process. It is in fact far more conducive to a better academic environment. It is more conducive to study, to higher grades, to concentrating. And that is understood: that is an age, especially from the age of, let's say, 13 to 18 and even beyond this, where you're bringing together two opposites that are definitely going to attract, and it does have its share of dangers.

Now, of course, this is not to address your particular question, because you are not in control of the society you're in. I'm merely pointing this out, especially for my audience that finds this question strange or troubling. And I do have members of my audience from all sides of the spectrum, where sometimes the question itself is too liberal or too conservative or whatnot, and again, I'm somebody who's trying to cater to many different audiences here. And my point is that I understand you problematize the question: "Oh my God, how can somebody ask about such a simple question? Of course genders should be interacting together." And my response is that, well, that's the society you and I have been born into. That's a society where the concept of gender segregation is almost unheard of.

Dare I say, almost nobody of the next generation can even imagine a society where genders are pushed to not necessarily just be together, where there should be a natural segregation, if not an actual segregation, which is enforced in some Gulf countries. The Shari'ah without a doubt would suggest some form of natural, healthy segregation when there's no need to be intermixing. The very notion of gender segregation, the very notion of having men and women not necessarily completely intermixed with one another, is alien to many people who are listening to this question, because they've never imagined or seen or visualized a society where that is possible.

As somebody who's lived in both types of societies, where gender segregation was harshly enforced and where there's complete intermixing, let me tell you honestly: there are definitely very major pros and cons in both of these. There's no question about that. There are major pros and cons; it's not that simplistic. And the point is that we also need to understand that there is a lot of good as well, and perhaps the good is far more than the bad, where there is some type of segregation that is there.

And we see this in simple statistics of our society and our time and our place. It is estimated, according to some latest surveys, that up to 60% of teenagers of high school (we're talking about high school), up to 60% of them, are engaging in premarital intercourse. This is in America. That is a staggering statistic. You're talking about 17-year-olds, 16-year-olds, and more than half of them are engaging in premarital... What do you think is going to happen? What do you think that's going to cause? Is that something that is healthy or not? And by the way, of that, around 5% or so are actually in middle school, basically below the age of 13; they are beginning. I mean, what is going to happen when you have daily interactions between the genders at this age, and the hormones are just coming in? Is that something that is really the wisest or not?

So, all of this having been said, the sister's asking a very specific question, and I'm saying it is halal and permissible. I still point out that we should also understand the Shari'ah does have a lot of wisdom, and even if some things might be permissible (it's permissible to interact in public with the opposite gender), still some amount of healthy segregation, without going overboard. Because again, we definitely have to take into account that a harsh segregation is counterproductive in a society where that segregation does not take place.

And I've spoken about this in other areas and issues, but again, to be very clear: in lands where gender segregation is unheard of, to try to force a very strict segregation within our communities and within our masajid is completely counterintuitive and counterproductive, because, especially given the technology and whatnot, it's not going to achieve its goal. Rather, what I'm suggesting is a healthy and organic segregation. And that's something that every community should come together and have a very frank discussion about, a very open discussion between the two genders, and various age segments as well, very important. You bring the young men and women, you bring the elders, and you have a frank conversation: okay, should we have a barrier or not, for example? Should we have this and that, for example?

In the time of the Prophet, men and women would be entering from one door. And Umar ibn al-Khattab, radiAllahu anhu, suggested, he said, "O Messenger of Allah, why don't we assign that door to the women and that door to the men?" And the Prophet readily agreed. So here's that organic segregation: why should men and women be jostling and shoving through the same door? They weren't able to, or the idea didn't come in the beginning; if they're able to, let's say, have two separate doors... We know that in the time of the Prophet ﷺ there was not a physical barrier, but the women were at the back and the men were at the front. That's a natural and healthy segregation. It's not something that is enforced by a wall.

And in fact, it is authentically narrated that a lady was having trouble hearing what the Prophet ﷺ said, so she leaned forward and she said, "Dear brother, may Allah have mercy on you, what did the Prophet ﷺ say?" And the brother leaned back and answered, "Oh, he said such and such." This is an authentic hadith in Muslim and others, that the lady said, "I couldn't hear what the Prophet ﷺ said, so I leaned forward and said, 'May Allah have mercy on you, can you tell me?'" That shows that there's just a barrier... I mean, not a barrier, a space between them, but there was interaction going on, and there's nothing wrong with that. Why should there be something wrong with that?

So my point being, the sister is asking a question; the response is very straightforward, that it is in fact not problematic at all. That having been said, it raises the broader question about gender interaction and ikhtilat, what is called in Arabic ikhtilat. And the response is that in and of itself, as Imam al-Nawawi said, an amount of intermixing is natural and a part of society; in and of itself it is not haram. Nonetheless, one should be aware that the Shari'ah does understand that just unbridled mixing, let's say, is not something that is healthy. It is not the default. And we should try our best to be reasonable in this regard: given the circumstances of society, take into account the norms of our Shari'ah, and have a middle ground in our communities and our masajid. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
